title: Viruses
summary: What all viruses have in common, how diverse they are, how bacteriophage lambda reproduces by lytic and lysogenic cycles, where viruses may have come from, and why they evolve so fast.

keyterms.definition: A small, non-cellular infectious particle of nucleic acid in a protein coat that can only reproduce inside a host cell.
The protein coat surrounding a virus's genetic material, made of repeating protein subunits.
An outer lipid membrane derived from the host cell's plasma membrane, with embedded viral proteins, present in some viruses such as HIV.
An organism or agent that can only reproduce inside a host cell, using the host's ribosomes, enzymes and ATP.
A virus that infects bacteria, e.g. lambda phage, which has double-stranded DNA in a protein head with a tail.
An RNA virus, such as HIV, that uses reverse transcriptase to make a DNA copy of its genome, which is inserted into the host's DNA.
Viral reproductive cycle in which the virus replicates in the host cell and new virions are released by lysis, killing the cell.
Viral cycle in which viral DNA integrates into the host chromosome and is copied with it at each division, without killing the host.
Phage DNA integrated into the bacterial chromosome during the lysogenic cycle.
Bursting of the host cell, releasing new virus particles.
Virus-first, progressive (escaped cellular genes) and regressive (reduced from cells) hypotheses; diversity suggests viruses arose more than once.
Changes in viral surface antigens, by gradual mutation (drift) or exchange of genome segments between strains (shift), as in influenza.
Rapid accumulation of mutations, especially in RNA viruses that lack proofreading, combined with short generation times and huge numbers.

questions.prompt: Which feature is common to all viruses?
options: A lipid envelope
Double-stranded DNA
Genetic material enclosed in a protein capsid
70S ribosomes
questions.explanation: All viruses have nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) inside a protein capsid. Only some have an envelope, many have RNA, and none have ribosomes.

questions.statement: Viruses have no cytoplasm and few or no enzymes of their own.
questions.explanation: Viruses lack cytoplasm and metabolism, so they must use the host cell's ribosomes, enzymes and ATP to replicate.

questions.prompt: Match each virus to its features.

pairs.right: Double-stranded DNA, head and tail, no envelope
Single-stranded RNA, enveloped with spike proteins
RNA retrovirus with reverse transcriptase, enveloped

questions.explanation: Viruses differ in nucleic acid type (DNA or RNA, single- or double-stranded) and in whether they have an envelope.

questions.text: In the lysogenic cycle, lambda DNA integrated into the bacterial chromosome is called a ___.
questions.explanation: The prophage is replicated along with the bacterial chromosome each time the cell divides.

questions.prompt: Put the stages of the lytic cycle of lambda phage in order.
items: Phage attaches to receptors on the bacterial cell
Phage DNA is injected into the host cell
Host machinery replicates phage DNA and makes phage proteins
The cell lyses, releasing new phages
questions.explanation: In the lytic cycle the phage takes over the host to make copies of itself, ending with lysis that kills the host.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes the lysogenic cycle from the lytic cycle?
options: In the lysogenic cycle viral DNA integrates into the host chromosome and the host is not immediately killed
In the lysogenic cycle the virus never enters the host cell
The lysogenic cycle produces new virions immediately by lysis
Only RNA viruses can enter the lysogenic cycle
questions.explanation: In lysogeny lambda DNA becomes a prophage and is passed to daughter cells. Later it can be induced to leave the chromosome and enter the lytic cycle.

questions.statement: A viral envelope is made by the virus from its own genes for lipid synthesis.
questions.explanation: The envelope lipid comes from the host cell's membrane as the virus buds out; only the embedded glycoproteins are coded for by viral genes.

questions.prompt: Why are viruses described as obligate intracellular parasites?
options: They live inside the nucleus of all cells
They can only reproduce inside a host cell using its machinery
They always kill the cell they infect
They are made of cells
questions.explanation: Without ribosomes or metabolism, a virus cannot make proteins or copy its genome outside a host. Lysogenic viruses do not immediately kill their host.

questions.text: The protein coat of a virus is called the ___.
questions.explanation: The capsid is made of protein subunits; an envelope (when present) is a lipid layer outside it.

questions.prompt: What can trigger a lambda prophage to switch from the lysogenic to the lytic cycle?
options: Addition of glucose
Infection by a second phage that is identical
Stress to the host cell, such as DNA damage
Integration of a second prophage
questions.explanation: When the host is stressed (e.g. DNA damage from UV), the prophage is excised and enters the lytic cycle, producing new phages before the host dies.

questions.prompt: Match each hypothesis for the origin of viruses to its idea.

pairs.right: Viruses arose before or alongside the first cells
Viruses descend from cells that lost functions

questions.explanation: Several hypotheses exist; the diversity of viruses suggests they may have originated several times by different routes.

questions.statement: The great diversity of viruses suggests they all evolved from a single common viral ancestor.
questions.explanation: Viruses share few genes and differ widely in genome type, which suggests several independent origins. Their shared features may reflect convergent evolution from their parasitic lifestyle.

questions.prompt: Which observation supports the idea that viruses originated from other organisms?
options: Viruses have their own unique genetic code
Viruses contain 80S ribosomes
Viruses can reproduce without host cells
Viruses use the same genetic code as their host cells
questions.explanation: Viruses use the universal genetic code and depend on host cells, consistent with them arising from cellular genetic material.

questions.text: The reverse transcriptase of HIV lacks proofreading, giving HIV a very high ___ rate.
questions.explanation: Without proofreading many errors arise in each copy, producing many variants on which natural selection acts.

questions.prompt: Why do viruses evolve so rapidly?
options: They reproduce sexually
High mutation rates, very short generation times and huge population sizes
They contain more genes than bacteria
Their capsids prevent mutations
questions.explanation: Many variants arise quickly and natural selection acts on enormous numbers of virions each generation, so allele frequencies change fast.

questions.statement: A new influenza vaccine is usually needed each year because the virus's surface antigens change.
questions.explanation: Antigenic drift (and occasionally shift) alters influenza surface proteins, so antibodies from earlier vaccines or infections may no longer recognise them.

questions.prompt: Why is HIV treated with a combination of several antiretroviral drugs at once?
options: It reduces the chance that a variant resistant to all the drugs will arise and be selected
Each drug kills a different type of host cell
A single drug would cure HIV too quickly
Antibiotics are included to destroy the capsid
questions.explanation: A variant would need mutations conferring resistance to every drug simultaneously, which is very unlikely, so resistance develops much more slowly.

questions.text: Exchange of genome segments between two influenza strains infecting the same cell is called antigenic ___.
questions.explanation: Shift is a sudden, major change that can create pandemic strains; drift is the gradual accumulation of point mutations.

questions.prompt: Order the steps by which a drug-resistant strain of a virus becomes common.
items: Random mutations produce variation among viruses
A drug is used to treat the infection
Resistant variants survive and replicate more
Resistant variants become the most common in the population
questions.explanation: Mutation creates variation first; the drug then acts as a selection pressure, so resistance alleles increase in frequency.

questions.prompt: Why are antibiotics not effective against viral infections such as influenza?
options: Viruses are too large for antibiotics to enter
Viruses always have an envelope
Antibiotics target bacterial structures and metabolism, which viruses do not have
Viruses evolve resistance to antibiotics instantly
questions.explanation: Antibiotics act on features such as bacterial cell walls and 70S ribosomes. Viruses have no metabolism of their own and use host cell machinery.
